newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish opposition's anti-Islamist move falters.
newsitem.headline: Turkish opposition's anti-Islamist move falters.

text.p: Turkish opposition plans for anti-Islamist unity against Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan faltered on Wednesday, dampening a government crisis over the function of both religion and the military.
Veteran left-wing leader Bulent Ecevit acknowledged that two other opposition figures had only loosely agreed to a plan to replace Islamist Erbakan's coalition with a secularist alliance.
"(Main opposition leader Mesut) Yilmaz found the idea of a broad-based government too ambitious," Ecevit told MPs from his Democratic Left Party.
He also said leftist rival Deniz Baykal had not given a clear reply in a round of talks on Tuesday to his call for a shadow government that would oust Erbakan.
The prime minister has come under heavy fire from Turkey's secularist power centres, led by the influential army, for plans to introduce Islam into public life.
Erbakan challenged his critics on Tuesday to elections but many MPs in both the opposition and his Islam-based Welfare Party are wary of losing their seats at early polls.

"We are not in a situation whereby early elections are needed," Welfare deputy chairman Riza Ulucak told a news conference. "However we would favour early elections to expose bare-faced liars," he said.
Stocks in Istanbul were down 0.49 percent in mid-afternoon but trading was light. Brokers said many investors have run for the sidelines amid mounting uncertainty.
Welfare took advantage of secularist disunity last year to become the first Islamist grouping to take power in Turkey's modern history.

It won a narrow victory with 21 percent of the vote at the last polls in late 1995. Many analysts say the Islamists' public support has probably risen since then, but reliable figures are difficult to come by.

Erbakan has stalled on intense demands from the military to reverse a rise in Islamic sentiment under his rule. A top general warned on Tuesday that Islamist extremism was a matter of "life or death" for the country.
The military has toppled three governments in the last 37 years but it has said it will not stage a coup this time around for fear of upsetting NATO member Turkey's Western allies.
The security establishment this week began a crackdown on outlawed Islamist activities regardless of Erbakan.

Police have closed dozens of unlicensed illegal religious education centres and Ankara state security court put a top Moslem preacher close to Welfare on trial for allegedly advocating harsh Islamic rule in Turkey.
The same court on Wednesday heard the case of more than 120 members of an Islamist sect charged with threatening Turkey's secular order.
"This is a political trial," said Cuneyt Toraman, a lawyer for the defendants, from the Aczmendi sect.

The Aczmendis grow long hair wrapped in turbans and carry staffs in what they say is imitation of the Prophet Mohammad. They were detained at a rowdy ceremony in Ankara last year at which they clashed with police.
